entries.topicDescription: Architecture component for managing UI-related data across configuration changes.

tips.title: StateFlow vs LiveData
tips.content:
Both StateFlow and LiveData hold observable state, but StateFlow
is Kotlin-first and works well with coroutines.

StateFlow always has a value (no null initial state).
It's lifecycle-unaware — use collectAsStateWithLifecycle() in Compose
or repeatOnLifecycle() in Views to collect safely.

LiveData is lifecycle-aware out of the box but predates coroutines
and doesn't integrate as naturally with coroutines and Flow.

tips.title: SavedStateHandle for process death
tips.content:
ViewModel survives rotation but NOT process death.
Android can kill your app's process in the background.

SavedStateHandle persists data across process death.
It acts like a map — get/set values that are saved to
the saved-state bundle automatically.

Use it for: search queries, selected tab index,
scroll position — anything the user would expect to survive.

tips.title: ViewModel basics — survive rotation
tips.content:
ViewModel stores and manages UI-related data. It survives
configuration changes like screen rotation.

A ViewModel is scoped to an Activity or Fragment. It's created
the first time the scope requests it and lives until the scope
is permanently destroyed (e.g., Activity finishes).

Put UI state and business logic calls in the ViewModel.
Keep the Activity/Fragment thin — just observing and rendering state.

tips.title: onCleared marks the end of a ViewModel's life — not a rotation
tips.content:
A ViewModel lives as long as its owner (an Activity, a Fragment or a navigation back stack entry) is in the back stack, and it survives configuration changes such as rotation. It is cleared only when the owner is permanently gone: the Activity finishes, the Fragment is removed or the destination is popped.

Then onCleared() is called, right after viewModelScope has been cancelled. Use it to release things the ViewModel created itself (a listener, a manually created scope, a resource) and keep it short.

tips.title: Never keep an Activity, View or Context in a ViewModel
tips.content:
A ViewModel outlives the Activity or Fragment that displays it: after a rotation the old Activity is destroyed but the same ViewModel lives on. If the ViewModel holds a reference to that Activity, a View or an Activity Context, the destroyed Activity can't be garbage collected, which leaks memory and the whole view tree.

Keep UI objects out of the ViewModel and expose state for the UI to render. If you truly need the application Context, extend AndroidViewModel, or better, inject a dependency that wraps it, such as a repository or a resource provider.

tips.title: Expose read-only state with a private backing property
tips.content:
Keep the MutableStateFlow private and expose it as a read-only StateFlow. The UI can then observe the state but only the ViewModel can change it, so every change goes through the ViewModel's functions and can be reasoned about in one place.

Change the state with update { }, which applies the function atomically. That avoids the lost-update problem of reading value and writing it back separately when several coroutines change state.

tips.title: Create ViewModels that need constructor arguments with a factory
tips.content:
The default ViewModel factory can only call a no-argument constructor. To pass dependencies, supply a factory. With plain AndroidX, viewModelFactory { initializer { } } builds one, and inside the initializer createSavedStateHandle() gives you a SavedStateHandle. Dependency-injection libraries wrap this for you.

Hilt uses @HiltViewModel with an @Inject constructor and hiltViewModel() in Compose; Koin has koinViewModel(). Whichever you use, the ViewModel's own constructor stays plain Kotlin, which keeps it easy to create in tests.

tips.title: Share one ViewModel between screens by choosing its owner
tips.content:
A ViewModel is scoped to the owner you ask it from. Ask from a destination and each screen gets its own. To share state across several screens of a flow, such as a multi-step checkout, use the owner that covers them all: the parent navigation graph's back stack entry, or the Activity.

Scoping to the navigation graph is usually better than to the Activity, because the ViewModel is cleared when the user leaves the flow instead of living for the whole session.

tips.title: Model one-time UI events as state the UI consumes
tips.content:
Things like "show this message" or "navigate now" must happen once. Firing them through a callback or a stream that drops values can lose them if the UI isn't collecting at that moment. A more robust approach recommended for Compose is to keep the event in the UI state until the UI reports that it handled it.

The ViewModel sets a field such as userMessage; the screen shows it and calls a function that clears it. Because state survives rotation, the event isn't lost, and because it is cleared after handling, it isn't shown twice.

tips.title: Work that must finish belongs outside viewModelScope
tips.content:
viewModelScope is cancelled as soon as the ViewModel is cleared, for example when the user leaves the screen. A save, an upload or a payment confirmation launched there can be cancelled halfway, leaving data in an inconsistent state.

For work that must complete, hand it to something with a longer life: WorkManager for work that must survive process death, or an application-level scope (injected, with a SupervisorJob) for short work that only needs to outlive the screen.

tips.title: Start loading with stateIn and onStart instead of in init
tips.content:
Calling a load function in a ViewModel's init block starts work as soon as the ViewModel is created, whether or not anything is observing it, and that work isn't restarted if it stops. Building the state from a Flow with stateIn(started = SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000)) ties the work to the observers instead: it starts when the UI starts collecting, keeps running through a configuration change, and stops five seconds after the last collector leaves.

It also makes the initial state explicit (onStart or the initial value) and is easier to test, because nothing happens until you collect.
